screens.title: Understanding ROS Services
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn what ROS services are, why they exist, and when to choose them over topics or actions. Services let one node ask a question and receive a direct answer—think of asking the robot “What is the battery level?” or “Toggle that LED.” They are synchronous: the client sends a request and waits until a server returns a response. That blocking behavior is important because it makes services ideal for quick queries and short commands, but unsuitable for continuous streaming or long-running operations. We will see how a service is defined using a. srv file, how to add it to CMake so ROS generates language bindings, and how to implement servers and clients in both Python and C++. You will also practice using rosservice command-line tools to inspect and call services during testing. By the end of the chapter you will be able to design a simple service, implement the server and client, and choose appropriately between topics, services, and actions when architecting robot behavior. As you go, pay attention to blocking versus non-blocking choices and test services with the terminal before wiring them into your system.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Understanding ROS Services
Understanding ROS Services
Synchronous request-response communication for fast, discrete robot tasks.

Services are the pattern you choose when a node needs an immediate answer or confirmation. They behave like remote function calls: a client calls, waits, and receives a response. Use services for short tasks such as querying status or toggling hardware state. Avoid services for streaming or long-running operations where non-blocking behavior is required.

In this lesson
Service anatomy, .srv files, build steps
Learn to define, build, and implement services in Python and C++.
Coming up
CLI debugging
Use rosservice to list, inspect, and call services for testing.
Hands-on
Build a ComputeSum service
Implement servers and clients in Python and C++, then test cross-language calls.
Visual concept
Topics
One-way streaming: sensors, continuous data
Services
Synchronous request-response for quick queries
Actions
Async goals with feedback for long tasks
Key Takeaway

Use services for short, discrete interactions where a node must wait for an answer. For continuous or high-frequency data prefer topics; for long-running goals prefer actions.

screens.title: What is a ROS Service?
screens.narratorSegment: A ROS service is a synchronous request-response communication model where a client sends a request message and waits for a response from a server. Put simply, services are remote function calls in a distributed system. They are ideal for discrete operations that must complete quickly, such as querying the current battery level or toggling an LED. Because the client blocks until it receives the response, services are not suitable for streaming telemetry or tasks that may take a long time. One clear example from the chapter is asking "What is the current battery level?"—a single request that expects a single reply. A common misconception is treating services like topics; unlike topics, services are two-way and blocking. That blocking behavior means you must design servers to respond promptly and consider timeouts in clients. Another misconception is believing multiple servers can advertise the same service name—ROS allows one server per service name. Key practical consequences are simple: use services for short queries and confirmations, use topics for continuous data streams, and prefer actions for long-running tasks that need feedback and cancellation. Reflect: what discrete queries in your robot design would be better served by a service rather than a topic?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A service is a synchronous remote call: client sends request, blocks, and receives a response; best for short, discrete interactions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is a ROS Service?
Definition & claim

A service is a synchronous request-response interaction. The client sends a request message and blocks until the server returns a response. Services act like remote function calls across nodes in ROS.

Concrete example: Ask \'What is the current battery level?\' — the server replies with the numeric percentage and the client uses that value immediately.
Misconception check: Services are not streams. They are one-off, blocking calls. For continuous updates, use a topic.
Visual metaphor
Think of a service as a two-way street: you ask a question and wait for the reply before continuing.
Contrast: a topic is a one-way highway where messages flow continuously without waiting.
Key Takeaway

Use services for short, synchronous queries or commands that must return a confirmation or value immediately.

screens.title: Service name, request type, and response type
screens.narratorSegment: Every service is defined by three elements: a name, a request message type, and a response message type. The name is a string such as /get_battery_level or /set_led and acts as the single identifier nodes use to call or advertise the service. The. srv file is the contract: fields above the '---' belong to the request, and fields below are the response. For example, SetLed. srv includes an integer LED number and a boolean state in the request, and a boolean success with a message string in the response. This clear separation ensures both client and server agree on the shape and types of data exchanged. Practically, one server advertises the service name and publishes the implementation; multiple clients can call the service concurrently, and ROS serializes requests and responses for transport. A common design error is putting large or streaming data in a service; since clients block, large payloads increase latency and risk freezing callers. A better approach for heavy data is to use topics. Think of a. srv as a small contract: keep request and response compact and focused on the discrete information needed for the operation. How would you design a service contract for requesting robot pose confirmation?

keyIdea.title: Anatomy
keyIdea.text: Service = name + request fields + response fields. Keep fields small and focused; the .srv file is the contract both sides share.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Service Anatomy
The .srv contract
# File: srv/SetLed.srv
int32 led_number
bool state
---
bool success
string message
Request fields are above the separator and response fields are below. Keep fields concise so calls return quickly.
Process steps
  1. Define .srv with request and response fields.
  2. Add the .srv file to add_service_files() in CMakeLists.txt.
  3. Generate messages so both Python and C++ can import the types.
  4. Implement server and client using the generated types.
Design tip
Favor small, typed fields in .srv files. Avoid placing large blobs or streaming data in service requests or responses.

screens.title: Adding services to CMakeLists
screens.narratorSegment: To use a custom. srv file, you must add it to your package's build so ROS generates the language bindings. In CMakeLists. txt you declare a dependency on message_generation and list service files with add_service_files(). Then you call generate_messages() specifying any message dependencies. This process instructs catkin or colcon to generate Python and C++ types that code can import. Without this step, Python imports and C++ headers will not exist and your code will fail to build or import. A common mistake is forgetting to add message_generation in find_package or to include generate_messages after add_service_files. Another pitfall is failing to list necessary dependencies under generate_messages; missing dependencies will cause compilation errors. After correctly configuring CMake, build your workspace; you can confirm generated types exist by inspecting devel or install spaces or by using rosservice type and rosservice args to see the service signature. Keep your. srv files under the srv/ directory and treat them as the single source-of-truth for client and server message structures. This makes cross-language calls reliable because both sides use the same generated types. Adding services to CMakeLists means declare message_generation, add .srv files with add_service_files(), and call generate_messages() so python/c++ types are generated.. In practical terms, how message_generation and add_service_files integrate .srv into your build. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Adding services to CMakeLists
CMake snippet
find_package(catkin REQUIRED COMPONENTS
  ...
  message_generation
)

add_service_files(
  FILES
  SetLed.srv
)

generate_messages(
  DEPENDENCIES
  std_msgs
)
Add the service file here and list dependencies. Then rebuild so generated headers and Python modules are available.
Checklist
  • Place .srv file in srv/ directory.
  • Add message_generation to find_package.
  • Call add_service_files with your .srv filename.
  • Call generate_messages with any dependencies listed.
Common mistake
Forgetting to rebuild the workspace after adding .srv files. Always rebuild and verify the generated types before running nodes that import them.

screens.title: Writing a Python service server
screens.narratorSegment: A Python service server uses a callback that accepts the request and returns a response object. In rospy you create a Service using rospy. Service with the service name, service type, and handler. The handler receives an object whose fields match the request side of the. srv contract. Inside the handler you perform the requested action, log useful information, and return a response built from the generated response type. The server must call rospy. spin() to keep running and serving requests. The chapter example for SetLed demonstrates this pattern. Practically, keep the handler small and deterministic so calls return quickly. If the handler needs to perform longer work, consider offloading to a background thread and returning an immediate acknowledgement, or switch to an action interface. A concrete example: a handler that sets an LED and returns success and a formatted message. A common mistake is returning plain tuples or mismatched types; always return the generated response type. After implementing the server, verify it with rosservice call before writing the client. This ensures the server advertises the correct name and type, and that the handler returns the expected fields.

keyIdea.title: Python server
keyIdea.text: Use rospy.Service() to advertise a service; handler receives request, performs work, and returns a generated response object.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Python Service Server
Server example (visual)
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy
from my_first_robot.srv import SetLed, SetLedResponse

def handle_set_led(req):
  rospy.loginfo("Setting LED %d to %s", req.led_number, req.state)
  # control hardware here
  success = True
  message = "LED %d set to %s" % (req.led_number, req.state)
  return SetLedResponse(success, message)

if __name__ == '__main__':
  rospy.init_node('led_server')
  srv = rospy.Service('/set_led', SetLed, handle_set_led)
  rospy.loginfo("LED server is ready.")
  rospy.spin()
The handler returns a SetLedResponse instance. Use logging to record requests and avoid long blocking operations inside the handler.
Explanation
  • rospy.Service advertises the service to the ROS Master.
  • Handler receives a typed request object matching the .srv file.
  • Return the generated response type, not raw primitives.
Key Takeaway

Keep the handler simple and fast. Use the generated response type and verify with rosservice call.

screens.title: Writing a Python service client
screens.narratorSegment: A Python client interacts with a service by waiting for availability and then calling through a ServiceProxy. Use rospy. wait_for_service with the service name to block until the service is advertised. Then create a ServiceProxy that wraps the remote call and behaves like a local function. When you call the proxy, the call blocks until the server returns a response or an error occurs. The chapter example shows using rospy. ServiceProxy to call /set_led and capturing the returned success flag and message. Handle ServiceException to catch failures and log or retry as appropriate. For example, a client asking to set LED one to true will wait for the server, call it, and then print the response. A frequent beginner mistake is not waiting for the service and assuming it exists; this causes immediate errors. Another practical point is to avoid high-frequency polling of a service—use topics for repeated state checks. After calling the service, validate the returned values and handle false success flags or error messages by retrying or falling back to safe behavior. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Python Service Client
Client example (visual)
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy
from my_first_robot.srv import SetLed

def set_led_client(led_number, state):
  rospy.wait_for_service('/set_led')
  try:
    set_led = rospy.ServiceProxy('/set_led', SetLed)
    resp = set_led(led_number, state)
    return resp.success, resp.message
  except rospy.ServiceException as e:
    rospy.logerr("Service call failed: %s", e)
    return False, "Error"

if __name__ == '__main__':
  rospy.init_node('led_client')
  success, message = set_led_client(1, True)
  rospy.loginfo("Result: %s - %s", success, message)
wait_for_service ensures the service exists before calling. ServiceProxy behaves like a local function but performs a network call that blocks until a response arrives.
Notes
  • Handle ServiceException to detect call failures.
  • Do not call services at very high frequency—subscribe to topics instead.
  • Validate the response fields, such as success flags or message text.
Common pitfall
Calling a service that is not yet available. Always wait for the service or guard calls with availability checks.

screens.title: Writing a C++ service server
screens.narratorSegment: In C++ a service server uses advertiseService on a NodeHandle and a callback that receives Request and Response references. The callback fills response fields and returns true on success, signaling ROS to send the response back. The chapter example shows the handleSetLed function accepting typed request and response parameters, logging the action, setting response. success and response. message, and returning true. Remember to initialize ros::init and create a NodeHandle before advertising the service, and call ros::spin() to keep the node alive. A common C++ mistake is returning false from the callback or failing to populate response fields correctly, which results in clients receiving default values or a failed call. Also ensure your package generates the appropriate headers for the service type in CMakeLists and that you include the generated header in your code. Testing the C++ server with rosservice call or a Python client helps confirm the service signature and behavior are correct. The C++ approach is synchronous just like Python: clients block until the response returns, so keep the callback efficient and deterministic. Writing a C++ service server means use nh.advertiseservice with a callback that fills the response reference and returns a boolean indicating success.. In practical terms, callback signature and returning the response by reference. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

C++ server example
#include <ros/ros.h>
#include <my_first_robot/SetLed.h>

bool handleSetLed(my_first_robot::SetLed::Request& req,
                  my_first_robot::SetLed::Response& res) {
  ROS_INFO("Setting LED %d to %d", req.led_number, req.state);

C++ client example
#include <ros/ros.h>
#include <my_first_robot/SetLed.h>

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
  ros::init(argc, argv, "led_client");
  ros::NodeHandle nh;
  ros::ServiceClient client = nh.serviceClient("/set_led");
  ros::service::waitForService("/set_led");

  } else {
    ROS_ERROR("Failed to call service");
  }
  return 0;
}

screens.title: Topics vs Services vs Actions
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right communication pattern is a core design decision in ROS. Topics are publish-subscribe streams best for continuous sensor data or frequent command streams because they are non-blocking and many subscribers can listen simultaneously. Services are synchronous request-response interactions suited for one-off queries and quick commands that require an immediate result or confirmation. Actions are for long-running goals where you need goal, feedback, result, and the ability to cancel the operation. The chapter comparison table highlights blocking behavior: services block the client until the server replies; topics do not block; actions provide asynchronous feedback and do not block the caller. A practical example: battery level should be published on a topic at a low frequency rather than polled via a service every 100 milliseconds. A navigation node polling battery via a service at high frequency could introduce latency and jitter. When in doubt, ask: does the consumer need continuous updates, or only occasional confirmations? If continuous, use a topic. If a task takes time and needs progress updates, use an action. If a short, immediate answer is required, use a service. This decision affects responsiveness and system architecture.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn what ROS services are, why they exist, and when to choose them over topics or actions. Services let one node ask a question and receive a direct answer—think of asking the robot “What is the battery level?” or “Toggle that LED.” They are synchronous: the client sends a request and waits until a server returns a response. That blocking behavior is important because it makes services ideal for quick queries and short commands, but unsuitable for continuous streaming or long-running operations. We will see how a service is defined using a. srv file, how to add it to CMake so ROS generates language bindings, and how to implement servers and clients in both Python and C++. You will also practice using rosservice command-line tools to inspect and call services during testing. By the end of the chapter you will be able to design a simple service, implement the server and client, and choose appropriately between topics, services, and actions when architecting robot behavior. As you go, pay attention to blocking versus non-blocking choices and test services with the terminal before wiring them into your system.

These objectives guide the skills you'll practice while learning ROS services. First, you will explain the concrete difference between topics and services, including blocking behavior and appropriate use cases. Second, you will implement a service server in both Python and C++, learning how callbacks receive a request and return a response. Third, you will implement service clients in Python and C++, using the wait and call primitives correctly and handling failures. Fourth, you will use rosservice command-line tools to inspect, call, and debug services during development. Each objective includes a small practice: define a. srv file, build it, run a server, test it with rosservice call, and then build a client that consumes it. This sequence reinforces the language-agnostic nature of ROS services and gives you hands-on experience with both Python and C++ toolchains. By the end of the chapter you will understand when services are the right pattern and how to test them quickly from the terminal.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical skills you'll use in the lab. You will create a ComputeSum. srv file, implement a Python server that computes the sum of two integers, and write a Python client that requests the sum. You will test the service using rosservice call to quickly verify behavior. Then you will port the server and client to C++ and build with the package's CMakeLists so ROS generates language bindings. Finally you will test language interoperability by calling the C++ server from the Python client and vice versa. These steps show that ROS services are language-agnostic, because the. srv contract and ROS serialization allow different languages to interoperate. The lab reinforces good habits: keep service operations short, log results in the server, and handle service failure gracefully in the client. After completing the lab you should be comfortable adding service files to a package, generating messages, and exercising services from both code and the terminal.

A ROS service is a synchronous request-response communication model where a client sends a request message and waits for a response from a server. Put simply, services are remote function calls in a distributed system. They are ideal for discrete operations that must complete quickly, such as querying the current battery level or toggling an LED. Because the client blocks until it receives the response, services are not suitable for streaming telemetry or tasks that may take a long time. One clear example from the chapter is asking "What is the current battery level?"—a single request that expects a single reply. A common misconception is treating services like topics; unlike topics, services are two-way and blocking. That blocking behavior means you must design servers to respond promptly and consider timeouts in clients. Another misconception is believing multiple servers can advertise the same service name—ROS allows one server per service name. Key practical consequences are simple: use services for short queries and confirmations, use topics for continuous data streams, and prefer actions for long-running tasks that need feedback and cancellation. Reflect: what discrete queries in your robot design would be better served by a service rather than a topic?

Every service is defined by three elements: a name, a request message type, and a response message type. The name is a string such as /get_battery_level or /set_led and acts as the single identifier nodes use to call or advertise the service. The. srv file is the contract: fields above the '---' belong to the request, and fields below are the response. For example, SetLed. srv includes an integer LED number and a boolean state in the request, and a boolean success with a message string in the response. This clear separation ensures both client and server agree on the shape and types of data exchanged. Practically, one server advertises the service name and publishes the implementation; multiple clients can call the service concurrently, and ROS serializes requests and responses for transport. A common design error is putting large or streaming data in a service; since clients block, large payloads increase latency and risk freezing callers. A better approach for heavy data is to use topics. Think of a. srv as a small contract: keep request and response compact and focused on the discrete information needed for the operation. How would you design a service contract for requesting robot pose confirmation?

To use a custom. srv file, you must add it to your package's build so ROS generates the language bindings. In CMakeLists. txt you declare a dependency on message_generation and list service files with add_service_files(). Then you call generate_messages() specifying any message dependencies. This process instructs catkin or colcon to generate Python and C++ types that code can import. Without this step, Python imports and C++ headers will not exist and your code will fail to build or import. A common mistake is forgetting to add message_generation in find_package or to include generate_messages after add_service_files. Another pitfall is failing to list necessary dependencies under generate_messages; missing dependencies will cause compilation errors. After correctly configuring CMake, build your workspace; you can confirm generated types exist by inspecting devel or install spaces or by using rosservice type and rosservice args to see the service signature. Keep your. srv files under the srv/ directory and treat them as the single source-of-truth for client and server message structures. This makes cross-language calls reliable because both sides use the same generated types. Adding services to CMakeLists means declare message_generation, add .srv files with add_service_files(), and call generate_messages() so python/c++ types are generated.. In practical terms, how message_generation and add_service_files integrate .srv into your build. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Python service server uses a callback that accepts the request and returns a response object. In rospy you create a Service using rospy. Service with the service name, service type, and handler. The handler receives an object whose fields match the request side of the. srv contract. Inside the handler you perform the requested action, log useful information, and return a response built from the generated response type. The server must call rospy. spin() to keep running and serving requests. The chapter example for SetLed demonstrates this pattern. Practically, keep the handler small and deterministic so calls return quickly. If the handler needs to perform longer work, consider offloading to a background thread and returning an immediate acknowledgement, or switch to an action interface. A concrete example: a handler that sets an LED and returns success and a formatted message. A common mistake is returning plain tuples or mismatched types; always return the generated response type. After implementing the server, verify it with rosservice call before writing the client. This ensures the server advertises the correct name and type, and that the handler returns the expected fields.

A Python client interacts with a service by waiting for availability and then calling through a ServiceProxy. Use rospy. wait_for_service with the service name to block until the service is advertised. Then create a ServiceProxy that wraps the remote call and behaves like a local function. When you call the proxy, the call blocks until the server returns a response or an error occurs. The chapter example shows using rospy. For example, a client asking to set LED one to true will wait for the server, call it, and then print the response. Another practical point is to avoid high-frequency polling of a service—use topics for repeated state checks. After calling the service, validate the returned values and handle false success flags or error messages by retrying or falling back to safe behavior. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing the right communication pattern is a core design decision in ROS. Topics are publish-subscribe streams best for continuous sensor data or frequent command streams because they are non-blocking and many subscribers can listen simultaneously. Services are synchronous request-response interactions suited for one-off queries and quick commands that require an immediate result or confirmation. Actions are for long-running goals where you need goal, feedback, result, and the ability to cancel the operation. The chapter comparison table highlights blocking behavior: services block the client until the server replies; topics do not block; actions provide asynchronous feedback and do not block the caller. A practical example: battery level should be published on a topic at a low frequency rather than polled via a service every 100 milliseconds. A navigation node polling battery via a service at high frequency could introduce latency and jitter. When in doubt, ask: does the consumer need continuous updates, or only occasional confirmations? If continuous, use a topic. If a task takes time and needs progress updates, use an action. If a short, immediate answer is required, use a service. This decision affects responsiveness and system architecture.

This hands-on activity walks you through building a ComputeSum service that takes two integers and returns their sum. Add the file to add_service_files in CMakeLists and call generate_messages with appropriate dependencies. Rebuild the workspace so the generated types are available. Here are the core ideas to carry forward. Services are synchronous request-response communications best for quick queries and one-off commands. A. srv file defines the request and response fields separated by a separator; treat it as the contract shared by clients and servers. You must add service files to CMakeLists and call generate_messages so ROS generates language-specific types for Python and C++. Implement servers that return the generated response types and clients that wait for and call services using the provided primitives. Use rosservice command-line tools for quick inspection and testing before wiring clients into your system. Finally, design your architecture carefully: prefer topics for continuous or high-frequency data, services for short queries, and actions for long-running goals that need feedback and cancellation. Keep handlers fast and avoid polling services at high frequency. These practices lead to predictable, responsive robot systems.

Keep these three concise rules in mind as you design with ROS services. First, services are synchronous and block the caller, so use them for quick, infrequent queries and confirmations. Second, the. srv file is the single contract that both client and server share; add it to your build so types are generated for all languages you use. Third, prefer topics for streaming data and actions for long-running tasks with feedback. Use rosservice tools to test early and avoid integrating untested services into running systems. These rules help you design responsive, maintainable robot behaviors. As you build the lab, verify each step from the terminal and consider whether a service is the best fit for each requirement you encounter.
